drapeaux.note: The two phrases attributed to the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia (“wholly lacking in critical spirit” and “favorite manual”) are translated back from the French; the English text of the encyclopedia was not retrieved, so the published wording may differ (original not retrieved).

titre: Pope Joan: A 13th-Century Legend Mistaken for a Chronicle
accroche: A woman on the throne of Saint Peter around 855: no contemporary mentions her, and the chronology rules her out.
contenu_vulgarise:
According to a story long repeated, a 9th-century pontiff, known as John the Englishman, was a woman. She is said to have died in childbirth in the middle of a procession. The sources of the time are silent, and for good reason: the story dates from four centuries later.

## A Story That Changes Century

The oldest known mention of a woman pope appears in the *Chronica universalis Mettensis* of Jean de Mailly, around 1250; the figure is anonymous there. The Dominican Stephen of Bourbon takes up the story. It spread above all through the third edition, running to 1277, of Martin of Troppau's *Chronicle of the Popes and Emperors*, a widely read history manual of the late Middle Ages. This version adds a name, John the Englishman of Mainz, and a century: the female pope is said to have reigned between Leo IV and Benedict III, in the 850s. The 1913 *Catholic Encyclopedia* judges Martin's work “wholly lacking in critical spirit” and notes that the fable owes its wide diffusion to it.

## What the Chronology Forbids

Leo IV died on July 17, 855, and Benedict III was elected immediately after his death: the calendar leaves no room for a pontificate between the two. The legend has to find a place that the calendar does not leave it.

It has nevertheless left material traces. In Siena cathedral, a bust bore the inscription “Johannes VIII, Foemina de Anglia” among the gallery of popes; around 1600, it was turned into a bust of a male pope, and in 1601, Clement VIII declared the legend false.

The medium matters: Martin's chronicle, a “favorite manual” of the late Middle Ages according to the *Catholic Encyclopedia*, lines up the popes on one page and the emperors opposite, one line per year. An anecdote that appears there reads like one link in the list of popes, not like a rumor.

## What This Changes

Who destroys the legend? Not a defender of the papacy, but a Protestant. The Huguenot David Blondel published in 1647 a treatise that dismantles its chronology, and his conclusion is now generally accepted. The case shows that a story can survive four centuries in chronicles, and even in the decor of a cathedral, without any contemporary source to support it.

It is not the absence of a female pope that is striking, it is the age of the belief.

repere.texte: Leo IV died on July 17, 855, and Benedict III was elected immediately after his death: there is no place for a pontificate of “John the Englishman” between the two.

carte.punch: Pope Joan was born in 13th-century chronicles, four centuries after her supposed reign.
carte.idee: First mention around 1250, spread by Martin of Troppau's chronicle (to 1277). Leo IV died on July 17, 855, and Benedict III was elected immediately after his death. It was a Protestant, David Blondel (1647), who dismantled the legend.

quiz.question: Why do historians rule out the existence of a female pope around 855?
choix: Because Benedict III was elected immediately after the death of Leo IV, on July 17, 855
Because the Vatican destroyed all the archives of this period
Because Jean de Mailly, who cites her first, specifies that it is a fiction
Because the chroniclers of the time hid her out of modesty
quiz.explication: It is the chronology that rules her out: Benedict III was elected immediately after the death of Leo IV, with no room for an intervening pontificate. No destruction of archives is established, and Jean de Mailly reports the story as fact, not as fiction.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who dismantled the legend of the female pope in a 1647 treatise?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Blondel, a Protestant, dismantled the story's chronology. Clement VIII merely declared the legend false in 1601, and Martin of Troppau, on the contrary, spread the fable.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What is Martin of Troppau's role in this story?
choix: He is the oldest source, as early as the 9th century
His widely read manual gave the legend a name and a date, and spread it widely
He investigated and concluded it was false
He had the bust in Siena cathedral sculpted
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The oldest known mention is earlier, around 1250 in Jean de Mailly. Martin, whose manual was widely read, did not contest the story but spread it. The bust is not his doing.
